title: Week 36 · Lesson 60: Obesity Medicine & Metabolic Pharmacology — FNP-Level Prescribing, Monitoring & Referral
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 36 — Lesson 60: Obesity Medicine & Metabolic Pharmacology

FNP-level goal: Treat obesity as a chronic, multifactorial disease; select medication only after a respectful diagnostic and safety assessment; recognize drug-specific contraindications, adverse effects, interactions, and red flags; and coordinate nutrition, behavioral, medical, and bariatric care without stigma.

Learning Objectives

  • Use a weight-inclusive, nonstigmatizing assessment that identifies obesity-related complications and contributors to weight change.
  • Explain how incretin-based, sympathomimetic, absorption-blocking, and combination medications differ in mechanism and risk.
  • Screen for pregnancy, eating disorder concerns, substance use, psychiatric risk, cardiovascular disease, renal/hepatic disease, and medication interactions before prescribing.
  • Recognize dehydration, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, hypoglycemia, mood change, and other symptoms that require urgent reassessment.
  • Build a follow-up plan around health outcomes, tolerability, nutrition, muscle preservation, access, and patient goals—not a number on the scale alone.
  • Know when to coordinate endocrinology, obesity medicine, nutrition, behavioral health, sleep medicine, or bariatric surgery evaluation.

Part 1 — Obesity Care Starts With Respectful Clinical Reasoning

Obesity is a complex chronic disease influenced by biology, environment, access to food and activity, sleep, stress, medications, mental health, genetics, social context, and prior treatment experiences. Weight is a clinical data point, not a moral judgment. Ask permission to discuss weight, use person-first language when preferred, and define the patient’s goals: mobility, energy, glycemic control, blood pressure, sleep, pain, fertility, prevention, or quality of life may matter more than a specific weight target.

BMI can help identify risk and determine eligibility under product labeling, but it does not describe body composition, fat distribution, functional status, or the cause of weight change. Assess waist-related cardiometabolic risk when appropriate and screen for hypertension, diabetes/prediabetes, dyslipidemia, MASLD, obstructive sleep apnea, osteoarthritis, GERD, infertility/PCOS, depression, and cardiovascular disease. Unintentional weight loss, rapid gain with edema, Cushingoid features, thyroid symptoms, or concerning GI symptoms change the differential and should not be managed as routine obesity treatment.

Part 2 — Before Prescribing, Find the Drivers and the Risks

Take a weight timeline: childhood pattern, recent changes, pregnancies, injuries, shift work, sleep, stress, food insecurity, alcohol, substance use, prior diets, prior medications, and prior procedures. Reconcile every medication. Some therapies can contribute to weight change, while an unplanned medication change may destabilize diabetes, mood, seizures, HIV, transplant care, or another serious condition. The FNP task is to identify options and coordinate changes safely, not simply stop a medicine because weight gain is possible.

Screen for binge-eating symptoms, purging, severe restriction, depression, suicidality, substance use, and body-image distress. Medication is not a substitute for diagnosing an eating disorder or addressing acute behavioral-health risk. Obtain a focused history and targeted tests that answer a question; do not order a broad endocrine panel for every patient without clinical clues.

Part 3 — Medication Is an Adjunct, Not a Test of Willpower

FDA-approved chronic weight-management medications are used with nutrition, physical activity, behavioral support, and treatment of related disease. For many adults, labeling-based use is considered at BMI 30 kg/m² or greater, or BMI 27 kg/m² or greater with a weight-related condition; exact eligibility, age limits, dosing, and contraindications vary by product and must be verified in current labeling.

Medication response is variable. A patient who has little weight change may still have improvement in glycemia, blood pressure, mobility, cravings, or sleep; conversely, an impressive early scale response does not make dehydration, malnutrition, adverse effects, or unsafe dosing acceptable. Establish measurable health outcomes and reassess benefit, harm, affordability, access interruptions, and adherence at planned intervals.

Part 4 — Incretin-Based Therapy: Mechanism and Expectations

GLP-1 receptor agonists act through incretin pathways that influence appetite, food intake, insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent manner, glucagon physiology, and gastric emptying. Tirzepatide activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. These medicines can support substantial weight reduction for some patients, but they are not interchangeable across diabetes and obesity indications, doses, formulations, or insurance coverage.

Start and titrate only according to the exact product instructions and the patient’s tolerance. Early nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, dyspepsia, and reduced appetite are common and may improve with slower titration, hydration, smaller meals, and review of concurrent medicines. Severe, persistent, or progressive symptoms are not an instruction to simply push through to the next dose.

Part 5 — Incretin Safety: Think Beyond Nausea

Before and during incretin-based therapy, assess prior pancreatitis history and current abdominal symptoms, gallbladder disease symptoms, severe gastrointestinal disease, renal vulnerability during volume loss, diabetic retinopathy context in people with diabetes, and the product-specific contraindications and warnings. A personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2 is a major contraindication for relevant GLP-1/GIP-GLP-1 products; confirm the actual product labeling rather than generalizing across all medicines.

Urgent reassessment is appropriate for severe persistent abdominal pain, repeated vomiting with inability to hydrate, signs of dehydration or acute kidney injury, jaundice, fever with right-upper-quadrant pain, or symptoms suggesting pancreatitis, biliary disease, obstruction, or another acute abdomen. Do not diagnose these conditions from a message alone; determine stability and arrange timely in-person/emergency evaluation when indicated.

Part 6 — Diabetes Medicines, Hypoglycemia, and Dose Coordination

Incretin-based medicines generally have low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk, but risk rises when they are used with insulin or an insulin secretagogue such as a sulfonylurea. Reduced intake, vomiting, renal dysfunction, and rapid changes in glucose-lowering therapy can further change risk. Review the full diabetes regimen, glucose pattern, hypoglycemia history, monitoring access, and sick-day plan before adding or titrating therapy.

Do not instruct a patient to independently stop basal insulin, skip all diabetes medicines during illness, or combine multiple incretin products. Coordinate a dose-adjustment plan with the clinician managing diabetes when complexity is high. Symptoms such as confusion, seizure, loss of consciousness, or inability to take carbohydrate safely require emergency treatment pathways.

Part 7 — Oral and Combination Options Need Different Safety Screens

Orlistat reduces intestinal fat absorption and can cause oily stools, urgency, and vitamin-related concerns. It is not appropriate for every patient with malabsorption or cholestatic disease, and the full medication/supplement list matters. Counseling should include realistic meal-related effects and the need to follow product-specific guidance.

Phentermine-containing therapy has sympathomimetic effects. Cardiovascular history, blood pressure, heart rate, anxiety, insomnia, glaucoma, hyperthyroidism, substance-use history, and interacting medications all matter. Phentermine/topiramate has additional teratogenic and neurologic considerations; pregnancy prevention and testing requirements must follow the exact product program and labeling.

Naltrexone/bupropion can be unsafe with uncontrolled hypertension, seizure disorders, certain eating disorders, opioid use, abrupt withdrawal from alcohol or sedative substances, or duplicate bupropion exposure. It can precipitate opioid withdrawal and block opioid analgesia. Ask specifically about prescribed, illicit, and medication-assisted opioid treatment before considering it.

Part 8 — Pregnancy, Lactation, Procedures, and Contraception

Weight-management medications are not used during pregnancy, and pregnancy intention should be discussed before initiating or renewing treatment. If pregnancy occurs or is planned, follow current product labeling and coordinate obstetric care promptly rather than improvising a taper from memory. Lactation, fertility treatment, and the patient’s reproductive goals also require product-specific counseling.

Delayed gastric emptying, GI symptoms, and medication-associated weight change can affect the timing or reliability of other oral therapies in specific circumstances. Pre-procedure medication instructions also vary by patient risk, procedure, and anesthesia team. Do not provide a universal “hold” instruction; communicate with the procedural/anesthesia team and follow current institutional and product guidance.

Part 9 — Nutrition, Lean Mass, and Long-Term Safety

Reduced appetite can make it difficult for some patients to meet protein, fluid, fiber, vitamin, and mineral needs. Ask about dizziness, fatigue, constipation, food aversion, weakness, hair changes, and limited access to nutritious food. A plan that includes resistance activity when medically appropriate, adequate protein and hydration, and dietitian support can help protect function and lean mass while weight changes.

Do not normalize rapid, unmonitored dose escalation, sharing pens, obtaining products from unverified sellers, or using a compounded product as if it were automatically equivalent to an FDA-approved formulation. Confirm the source, exact ingredients, concentration, instructions, and prescriber/pharmacy involvement. When supply or coverage changes, help the patient avoid unsafe interruptions, duplicate therapy, or counterfeit products.

Part 10 — When to Refer for Metabolic and Bariatric Care

Referral is not failure. Consider coordinated obesity-medicine, endocrinology, dietitian, behavioral-health, sleep-medicine, or bariatric-surgery evaluation when disease complexity, medication contraindications, severe obesity-related complications, eating-disorder concerns, treatment nonresponse, or patient preference exceed the safe scope of routine primary care. Metabolic/bariatric surgery requires its own multidisciplinary assessment and lifelong nutrition, medication, and follow-up planning.

Obstructive sleep apnea, uncontrolled diabetes, advanced liver disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, severe depression, or substance-use disorder do not automatically exclude treatment; they increase the need for deliberate coordination. The FNP should make the next safest step visible to the patient rather than letting complexity become abandonment.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: Diabetes, Insulin, and a New Incretin Prescription

A patient with type 2 diabetes uses basal insulin and a sulfonylurea and asks for a weekly obesity medication after seeing a social-media advertisement. They have frequent overnight lows and limited access to glucose-monitoring supplies.

FNP reasoning: do not start with a refill-style prescription. Confirm indication, exact product, contraindications, pregnancy possibility, current glucose data, hypoglycemia risk, food intake, renal status, and the complete diabetes regimen. Coordinate a written monitoring and dose-adjustment plan; education about symptoms and emergency treatment is part of the prescription.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Vomiting Is Not Always a Routine Side Effect

A patient who recently titrated an incretin-based medicine reports persistent vomiting, severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, dark urine, and inability to keep fluids down.

FNP reasoning: this may be more than expected nausea. Assess stability and arrange urgent evaluation for dehydration, acute kidney injury, pancreatitis, biliary disease, obstruction, or another acute abdominal process. Do not advise another dose or a routine follow-up message.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: Naltrexone/Bupropion and Hidden Opioid Exposure

A patient wants an oral weight-management medication and says they take no pain medicine. Medication reconciliation reveals a chronic opioid prescription from another clinician.

FNP reasoning: naltrexone can precipitate withdrawal and block opioid effects. Pause the prescribing decision, clarify all opioid exposure and treatment goals, and coordinate pain/addiction care rather than treating the medication list as a checkbox.

FNP Obesity-Medicine Safety Framework

  1. Ask permission and define goals: use respectful language; prioritize function and health outcomes.
  2. Assess contributors and complications: weight trajectory, sleep, medications, eating pattern, mental health, pregnancy, and cardiometabolic disease.
  3. Match medication to patient: verify indication, labeling, contraindications, interactions, route, access, and patient preference.
  4. Plan monitoring before the first dose: response, vitals, glucose when relevant, hydration, nutrition, adverse effects, and follow-up timing.
  5. Coordinate dose changes: especially insulin, sulfonylureas, opioids, psychiatric medicines, and complex comorbid disease.
  6. Escalate red flags: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, dehydration, jaundice, altered mental status, severe hypoglycemia, chest symptoms, or psychiatric emergency.

High-Yield Summary

Obesity: a chronic, multifactorial disease requiring respectful, individualized care.
BMI: supports risk/eligibility assessment but does not replace clinical context.
Medication: adjunct to nutrition, movement, behavioral support, and treatment of comorbid disease—not a substitute for them.
GLP-1/GIP-GLP-1 therapy: can reduce appetite and improve metabolic outcomes; product-specific dosing, contraindications, and monitoring are essential.
Hypoglycemia: risk increases when diabetes therapy includes insulin or secretagogues; coordinate doses and monitoring.
Oral agents: have distinct GI, cardiovascular, seizure, opioid, psychiatric, and reproductive safety screens.
FNP standard: prescribe only after medication reconciliation, reproductive/behavioral screening, a monitoring plan, and clear emergency instructions.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Medication selection, eligibility, titration, contraindications, pregnancy management, peri-procedure guidance, monitoring, and referral must follow current FDA labeling, authoritative guidelines, local policy, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
